Deribit’s public feed, captured first-party across thirteen exchange-native streams, and extended back to March 2020 by a licensed archive of the options chain. Both sources share one schema in the data lake that backtests and the Scenario Lab’s stress replay read. Live analytics read Deribit through their own collector; what research and production share is the code path. First-party capture The book, rebuilt Live and replay Governance Request access → How backtests use the lake The data lake at a glance Capture Deribit feed · 13 exchange-native streams Resolution Sub-second native · 1-minute chain grid History First-party capture + licensed archive (Mar 2020) Coverage Every strike, every expiry, BTC + ETH Perpetual BTC-perpetual book and trades (Jul 2019) Licensed data Internal use; clients get derived outputs Why it matters A backtest is only as honest as its history. The questions worth asking of a replay are about the data underneath it: where it came from, what it holds, and what happens where it holds nothing. First-party Captured by us Our own continuous capture of Deribit’s public feed, recorded sub-second and archived before any processing. Depth Back to March 2020 A licensed archive extends the options chain back to March 2020 and the BTC-perpetual to July 2019, in the same schema. Honesty Not held, not invented A window the lake does not hold greys out rather than being synthesised, and every captured or archived row records its source. Key features Two sources, one schema. Capture · 13 streams, including quotes trades order book DVOL index mark prices listings settlement estimates venue status Delivery prices are polled hourly over REST rather than streamed. Daily OHLCV is derived from the trade tape at query time, not captured as its own channel. First-party capture Captured first-party, quote by quote. Our own continuous capture of the exchange’s public feed — thirteen streams, quote by quote, delivery prices polled hourly — extended backward by a licensed historical archive, both normalised into the same schema. Kept as captured. Every quote, every trade, every book update we capture, held at its original timestamp. Nothing smoothed, nothing interpolated. Raw first. A message is archived before any processing, so the archive is the log and every downstream table is a regenerable view of it. Every update, every instrument. The capture reads Deribit’s raw channels, which deliver every update, across every instrument the exchange lists. Deribit’s history. Backtests replay Deribit history only, and the licensed archive is Deribit’s: the books market intelligence reads on other exchanges are live surfaces, not backtest inputs. What comes back Deribit options, first-party capture. The full-depth book, every strike and expiry. Deribit options, licensed archive. Top-of-book quotes, marks, implied vol, Greeks and open interest, on every ticker change, from March 2020. BTC-perpetual, licensed archive. The full-depth book and trades, from July 2019. The licensed perpetual history is BTC-only; where the lake holds no ETH-perpetual series, an ETH backtest reads the underlying price recorded on the option chain itself. Inside the lake The book, kept as it stood. The data lake can return the book as it stood at any moment it holds — every strike, every expiry, bid and ask: full depth across our own capture, top-of-book across the licensed archive. In the product, backtests read that history through the chain grid. A boundary-exact chain grid. The lake keeps the 1-minute chain grid the backtester replays: a grid row at minute M is the option’s state at M. No lookahead. The replay refuses any grid row received after its own minute, or venue-stamped more than a second after it; the instrument carries forward from its last honest boundary instead of taking a substitute price. What it does not do yet. The replay does not yet filter stale rows, or rows from an exchange halt or maintenance window. Live Deribit feed → collector → live analytics and the live paper index History Deribit feed → first-party capture → data lake → backtest and stress replay One code path in both strategy engine fill convention skew and term-structure filters The licensed archive joins the lake in the same schema, extending it back to March 2020. Live and replay Two captures, one code path. When live analytics and historical replay are wired separately, they drift. Here, on Deribit, both start from the exchange’s own feed — read live by the collector, and captured separately into the lake the replay reads — and the strategy engine, the fill convention and the skew and term-structure filters are one code path in both. One engine, so a change lands in both. The same strategy engine runs the live paper index and the historical replay, so a model change lands in both. One skew, one term structure. The 25-delta risk reversal and the term-structure slope come from one shared definition, used by the live regime engine and every replay alike. Differences are versioned, not hidden. Where the live and replay read paths have differed, the fix is versioned in the methodology. How a backtest uses it → Who sees what Licensed archive. Internal: backtesting, model calibration and research. First-party capture. Our own record of the exchange’s public feed. Clients and LPs. Derived outputs, never the raw third-party ticks. The archive informs the models; it is never exported. Governance Licensed data stays internal. Provenance stays on the row. The licensed archive is third-party data, used internally for backtesting, model calibration and research. Clients receive derived outputs — never a redistributable copy of the ticks. Provenance per row. Every captured or archived row in the lake records its source, and the analytics treat both sources identically. If we don’t hold it, it greys out. A window we don’t hold is never synthesised. The preset simply disables itself. A missing day is never invented. A backtest skips a day the lake cannot serve and names it on the backfill, rather than filling it in. Email reza@quantstrix.com for the methodology → From the exchange to the replay How a print reaches a backtest. 01 · capture Thirteen streams Deribit’s public feed, read first-party over WebSocket, with delivery prices polled hourly. 02 · archive Raw first Each message is archived before any processing. 03 · normalise One schema First-party capture and the licensed archive share one schema, each row marked with its source. 04 · grid Boundary-exact A 1-minute chain grid for the backtester; a row at minute M is the option’s state at M. 05 · replay Backtest and stress replay The backtest reads the grid; the Scenario Lab’s stress replay reads daily spot and DVOL. Questions Frequently asked What data does QuantStrix capture? Deribit’s live feed across 13 exchange-native streams (12 over WebSocket, plus delivery prices polled hourly), captured first-party at sub-second resolution covering every BTC and ETH strike and expiry, extended by a licensed options archive since Mar 2020. How far back does the historical data go? The licensed archive holds the Deribit options chain for every BTC and ETH strike and expiry since March 2020, and the BTC-perpetual full-depth order book and trades since July 2019. First-party capture continues it forward. A replay offers only the dates its deployment’s data lake holds, and not every deployment carries the archive: a trial deployment may replay first-party capture only. Do live analytics and backtests read the same data? They start from the same exchange, through two separate captures. Live analytics read Deribit live through the collector; backtests and stress replays read the data lake, which captures Deribit separately and, in a deployment that carries it, adds the licensed archive. The strategy engine, the fill convention and the skew and term-structure filters are one code path in both. Do clients receive the licensed historical data? No. The licensed archive is used internally, for backtesting, model calibration and research. Clients receive derived outputs, such as backtested NAV and track records, never a redistributable copy of the ticks. What happens when the data lake does not hold a window? Nothing is invented. A preset stress window is offered only if the lake holds dates inside it, and one it does not hold greys out. A backtest skips a day the lake cannot serve and names it on the backfill, rather than filling it in. See the history behind a backtest.
